## Quantitative Bias Analysis

* What if you become aware of a confounder after the data collection happens?
* Obtain estimates of the confounder's prevalence (in all exposure strata) and association with outcome.
<!-- E.g. internal validation studies, expert guesses, external estimates from literature. -->
* Impute ( = calculate a best guess) numbers of exposed and affected subjects for each value of the confounder.
* This usually requires simplifying assumptions (i.e. a *model*), and can be done using a formula (e.g. for risk ratio), step-by-step, or in simulation.

## QBA Example
Source: [Fox MP, MacLehose R, Lash TL. *Applying Quantitative Bias Analysis to Epidemiologic Data.*  Springer. 2021. 2nd Edition.](https://sites.google.com/site/biasanalysis/)

|    :---   | :---: | :---: |
| **$D_+$** |  $a$  |  $b$  |
| **$D_-$** |  $c$  |  $d$  |
|           |  $m$  |  $n$  |

Source: [Fox MP, MacLehose R, Lash TL. *Applying Quantitative Bias Analysis to Epidemiologic Data.*  Springer. 2021. 2nd Edition.](https://sites.google.com/site/biasanalysis/)

| | **Total** $E_1$ | **Total** $E_0$ | **$C_1$** $E_1$ | **$C_1$** $E_0$ | **$C_0$** $E_1$ | **$C_0$** $E_0$ |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **$D_+$** | $a$ | $b$ | $A_1$ | $B_1$ | $A_0$ | $B_0$ |
| **$D_-$** | $c$ | $d$ | $C_1$ | $D_1$ | $C_0$ | $D_0$ |
| | $m$ | $n$ | $M_1$ | $N_1$ | $M_0$ | $N_0$ |
